Neurology · published research

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

Three rat reports describe better fear-memory discrimination or fewer PTSD-like behaviors after early PBM. A separate repetitive blast-injury study found no improvement in cognitive or PTSD-related behavioral traits.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Three rat reports describe better fear-memory discrimination or fewer PTSD-like behaviors after early PBM. A separate repetitive blast-injury study found no improvement in cognitive or PTSD-related behavioral traits.

Summary of the Evidence

The PTSD category contains four unique publications, all rat experiments, from researchers in China and the United States. Three reports test PBM as an early or preventive intervention after a trauma-related model. One study tests repetitive low-level blast injury and reports no behavioral benefit. No human trial, review or laboratory-only study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study of PBM for post-traumatic stress disorder was identified. The term PTSD in this literature refers to animal behaviors after experimentally induced trauma, not diagnosed human PTSD.

Animal evidence

In rats, Li et al. reported that PBM applied soon after fear conditioning or memory recall changed contextual or cued fear behavior, and that early treatment in a repeated-trauma model prevented some PTSD-like behaviors (Li et al. 2021). A related underwater-trauma study also reported prevention of some memory and behavioral changes (Li et al. 2021). Zhao et al. reported prevention of PTSD-like outcomes after pulsed 810-nm treatment in rats (Zhao et al. 2023). By contrast, transcranial laser treatment did not improve cognitive or PTSD-related behavioral traits in rats exposed to repetitive low-level blast injury (Garcia et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo PTSD study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Reported interventions include transcranial near-infrared PBM around 810 nm, delivered either as a brief early treatment or as repeated exposure after an experimental trauma. Models differ in whether they use fear conditioning, underwater trauma or blast injury. Treatment timing and behavioral tests also vary, so a positive result in one model does not demonstrate a common preventive effect.

Interpretation

The rat literature suggests that early PBM can alter fear-related behavior in some trauma models, but a separate blast model was null. These findings do not establish prevention or treatment of PTSD in people. The lack of clinical evidence and differences between the animal models are the principal limits.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for preventing PTSD in people because all four publications are rat studies. Low within selected rat trauma models for preventing some fear-memory or behavioral changes.
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Three rat reports describe prevention or improvement after early treatment, while a repetitive blast-injury study found no improvement in cognitive or PTSD-related behavior. No human cohort has been studied. Translational work should define the timing and safety of treatment and then test symptom outcomes in controlled human studies.
